lessons.title: Why invest at all? Inflation explained
lessons.body:
Money kept idle slowly loses its power. This is **inflation**: prices of food, rent and travel rise over time.

**Example:** if inflation averages 6% a year, ₹100 today will buy only what about **₹56** buys today after 10 years. Your note still says ₹100, but it buys less.

A savings account paying 3% while prices rise 6% means you are getting poorer each year without noticing. Investing aims to grow money **faster than inflation**, so your future self can afford the same life.

**Key idea:** the real return is your return minus inflation. A 7% return with 6% inflation is only about 1% real growth.
ta: பணவீக்கம் (inflation) காரணமாக பணத்தின் மதிப்பு ஆண்டுதோறும் குறைகிறது.
6% பணவீக்கத்தில், இன்றைய ₹100 பத்து வருடங்களில் சுமார் ₹56 மதிப்புக்கே பொருட்கள் வாங்கும்.
முதலீட்டின் நோக்கம்: பணவீக்கத்தை விட அதிக வேகத்தில் பணத்தை வளர்ப்பது.

quiz.q: Your savings earn 4% a year and inflation is 6%. What is happening to your money's buying power?
options: It shrinks by about 2% a year

lessons.title: Compounding: the eighth wonder
lessons.body:
**Compounding** means your returns start earning returns of their own. Growth snowballs over time.

**Example:** ₹1,00,000 growing at 12% a year becomes about **₹9.6 lakh in 20 years**. Most of that growth happens in the last few years, which is why starting early matters more than starting big.

**Rule of 72:** divide 72 by the yearly return to estimate how many years it takes to double. At 12%, money doubles roughly every **6 years**.

**Key idea:** time in the market is your biggest advantage. Interrupting compounding (selling in panic, withdrawing early) is very costly.
ta: கூட்டு வட்டி (compounding): உங்கள் லாபமும் லாபம் சம்பாதிக்கிறது.
₹1 லட்சம் 12% வளர்ச்சியில் 20 ஆண்டுகளில் சுமார் ₹9.6 லட்சமாகிறது.
72 விதி: 72-ஐ வருடாந்திர வருமானத்தால் வகுத்தால், பணம் இரட்டிப்பாகும் ஆண்டுகள் கிடைக்கும்.

quiz.q: Using the Rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at 9% a year?

lessons.title: Emergency fund before investing
lessons.body:
Before you buy a single share, keep an **emergency fund**: money for job loss, medical bills or urgent repairs.

A common guideline is **3 to 6 months of essential expenses**, kept somewhere safe and easy to withdraw, such as a savings account, a sweep-in FD or a liquid fund.

Why it matters: without it, an emergency can force you to sell investments at a bad time, often when markets are falling.

**Key idea:** invest only money you will not need for at least 3 to 5 years.
ta: முதலீடுக்கு முன் அவசர நிதி (emergency fund) அவசியம்.
குறைந்தது 3 முதல் 6 மாத அத்தியாவசிய செலவுகளை பாதுகாப்பான இடத்தில் வைத்திருங்கள்.
3–5 ஆண்டுகள் தேவைப்படாத பணத்தை மட்டுமே பங்குகளில் முதலீடு செய்யுங்கள்.

quiz.q: Where is an emergency fund usually best kept?
options: In a safe, easy-to-withdraw place like a savings account or liquid fund

lessons.title: Risk and return go together
lessons.body:
Higher possible returns always come with higher risk. There is no safe investment that gives very high returns. Anyone promising that is a red flag.

**Roughly, from lower to higher risk:** savings account and FDs → government bonds → debt funds → large-company shares → mid and small-company shares.

**Diversification** means spreading money across many companies, sectors and asset types, so one bad event does not sink everything.

**Key idea:** match the risk to your goal's timeline. Money needed in 1 year should not be in shares; money for 15 years away can handle ups and downs.
ta: அதிக வருமானம் என்றால் அதிக ஆபத்தும் உண்டு.
'உத்தரவாத அதிக லாபம்' என்ற வாக்குறுதி ஒரு எச்சரிக்கை அறிகுறி.
பல நிறுவனங்கள், துறைகளில் பணத்தைப் பிரிப்பது (diversification) ஆபத்தைக் குறைக்கும்.

quiz.q: Someone offers a 'guaranteed 5% per month' return. What should you think?
options: It's a red flag for a scam

lessons.title: What is a share? NSE, BSE and SEBI
lessons.body:
A **share** is a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company grows its profits, the value of your share can grow, and you may receive **dividends**.

In India, shares trade on two exchanges: the **NSE** (National Stock Exchange) and the **BSE** (Bombay Stock Exchange). **SEBI** is the regulator that protects investors.

To invest you need a **demat account** (holds your shares electronically, at NSDL or CDSL) and a **trading account** with a broker. Indian trades now settle on **T+1**, one working day after you buy.

**Key idea:** when you buy a share, you are buying part of a business, not a lottery ticket.
ta: பங்கு (share) என்பது ஒரு நிறுவனத்தின் சிறிய உரிமைப் பகுதி.
இந்தியாவில் NSE, BSE ஆகிய இரண்டு பங்குச் சந்தைகள்; SEBI ஒழுங்குமுறை அமைப்பு.
முதலீடு செய்ய demat கணக்கும் trading கணக்கும் தேவை.

quiz.q: Which organisation regulates India's securities market?

lessons.title: Nifty and Sensex: what the indices mean
lessons.body:
An **index** tracks a group of shares to show how the market is doing overall.

- **Nifty 50:** 50 large companies listed on the NSE.
- **Sensex:** 30 large companies listed on the BSE.
- **Bank Nifty:** the major banking shares.

When news says "Nifty fell 1%", it means those 50 companies, weighted by size, fell about 1% on average.

**Key idea:** indices are a scoreboard. Watching them daily is optional; long-term investors care about the trend over years.
ta: Index என்பது பல பங்குகளின் மொத்த நிலையைக் காட்டும் அளவுகோல்.
Nifty 50: NSE-யின் 50 பெரிய நிறுவனங்கள்; Sensex: BSE-யின் 30 பெரிய நிறுவனங்கள்.
நீண்டகால முதலீட்டாளர்களுக்கு தினசரி ஏற்ற இறக்கம் முக்கியமல்ல.

quiz.q: How many companies are in the Sensex?

lessons.title: Why share prices move
lessons.body:
In the short term, prices move with **news, emotions and money flows**: results, interest rates, global events, rumours.

In the long term, prices tend to follow **business performance**: growing profits and cash flows.

The investor Benjamin Graham described the market as a **voting machine in the short run and a weighing machine in the long run**.

**Key idea:** a falling price is not always bad news about the business, and a rising price is not always good news. Look at what the business is doing.
ta: குறுகிய காலத்தில் செய்திகள், உணர்வுகள் விலையை நகர்த்துகின்றன.
நீண்ட காலத்தில் விலை நிறுவனத்தின் லாப வளர்ச்சியைப் பின்தொடர்கிறது.
விலை வீழ்ச்சி எப்போதும் வணிகம் மோசம் என்று அர்த்தமல்ல.

quiz.q: Over many years, what tends to drive a company's share price most?
options: Its business profits and cash flows

lessons.title: Dividends, bonus issues and splits
lessons.body:
- **Dividend:** a share of profit paid out in cash. Dividend yield = yearly dividend ÷ share price.
- **Bonus issue:** free extra shares (e.g. 1:1). You hold more shares, but the price adjusts down, so your total value is unchanged.
- **Stock split:** one share becomes several smaller ones (e.g. ₹10 face value into ₹2). Again, total value does not change.

**Key idea:** bonuses and splits change the number of shares, not the value of the business. Don't buy just because of them.
ta: Dividend: லாபத்தில் ஒரு பகுதி பணமாக வழங்கப்படுகிறது.
Bonus, split: பங்குகளின் எண்ணிக்கை கூடும், ஆனால் மொத்த மதிப்பு மாறாது.
Bonus/split அறிவிப்புக்காக மட்டும் பங்கு வாங்க வேண்டாம்.

quiz.q: After a 1:1 bonus issue, what happens to your total investment value (on day one)?

lessons.title: Mutual funds in plain words
lessons.body:
A **mutual fund** pools money from many investors and a professional manager invests it in shares, bonds or both. You own **units**; the price of a unit is the **NAV**.

Types you will hear about: **equity funds** (shares), **debt funds** (bonds), **hybrid funds** (both), and by company size, **large, mid and small cap**.

Benefits: instant diversification and professional management, even with ₹500.

**Key idea:** read the scheme's objective and risk level (the "riskometer") before investing.
ta: Mutual fund பலரின் பணத்தை ஒன்றாகச் சேர்த்து நிபுணர் முதலீடு செய்கிறார்.
ஒரு யூனிட்டின் விலை NAV எனப்படும்.
முதலீடு செய்வதற்கு முன் ஃபண்டின் நோக்கம், ஆபத்து நிலையைப் படியுங்கள்.

quiz.q: What is NAV in a mutual fund?
options: The price of one unit of the fund

lessons.title: SIP and rupee-cost averaging
lessons.body:
A **SIP** invests a fixed amount every month automatically. When prices are low you buy more units; when high, fewer. This is **rupee-cost averaging**, and it removes the stress of timing the market.

**Example:** ₹5,000 a month for 20 years, assuming 12% a year, could grow to about **₹50 lakh**, from ₹12 lakh invested.

**Key idea:** the habit matters more than the amount. Start small, increase your SIP when your income rises (a "step-up").
ta: SIP: மாதம் ஒரு நிலையான தொகையை தானாக முதலீடு செய்வது.
விலை குறைந்தால் அதிக யூனிட்கள், உயர்ந்தால் குறைவான யூனிட்கள் கிடைக்கும்.
₹5,000 மாதம் 20 ஆண்டுகள் (12% எனக் கொண்டால்) சுமார் ₹50 லட்சமாகலாம்.

quiz.q: What does rupee-cost averaging mean?
options: Always buying at the lowest price
Buying more units when prices are low and fewer when high, by investing a fixed amount regularly

lessons.title: Index funds and ETFs
lessons.body:
An **index fund** simply copies an index like the Nifty 50, instead of a manager picking shares. An **ETF** does the same but trades on the exchange like a share (for example, gold ETFs like GOLDBEES).

Because there is little active management, costs are usually **much lower**.

**Key idea:** many beginners start with a low-cost Nifty 50 index fund, as it gives them a slice of India's largest companies in one go.
ta: Index fund ஒரு index-ஐ (எ.கா. Nifty 50) அப்படியே பின்தொடர்கிறது.
ETF பங்கு போல சந்தையில் வாங்கி விற்கலாம்.
செலவு (expense ratio) பொதுவாக மிகக் குறைவு.

quiz.q: Why are index funds usually cheaper than actively managed funds?
options: They simply copy an index, so there is less management work

lessons.title: Expense ratio and direct vs regular plans
lessons.body:
The **expense ratio** is the yearly fee a fund charges, taken from your returns. Small differences grow huge over time.

**Example:** ₹10 lakh for 20 years, earning 11% after a 1% fee, becomes about ₹80.6 lakh. With a 0.3% fee (11.7% net) it becomes about ₹91.4 lakh: **₹10.8 lakh more**, just from lower fees.

**Direct plans** have no distributor commission, so their expense ratio is lower than **regular plans** of the same fund.

**Key idea:** costs are one of the few things you fully control.
ta: Expense ratio: ஃபண்ட் வசூலிக்கும் வருடாந்திர கட்டணம்.
0.7% வித்தியாசம் கூட 20 ஆண்டுகளில் லட்சக்கணக்கில் மாறும்.
Direct plan-களில் கட்டணம் Regular plan-ஐ விட குறைவு.

quiz.q: Which usually has a lower expense ratio?

lessons.title: Revenue, profit and margins
lessons.body:
- **Revenue (sales):** money the company earns from customers.
- **Net profit:** what remains after all costs, interest and tax.
- **Profit margin:** profit ÷ revenue.

**Example:** revenue ₹1,000 crore and profit ₹150 crore means a **15% margin**.

Look at the **trend over several years**: steadily growing revenue and stable or rising margins are healthy signs. One great quarter proves little.

**Key idea:** quarterly results are on the company's website and on NSE/BSE, free to read.
ta: Revenue: வாடிக்கையாளர்களிடமிருந்து வரும் வருமானம்; Net profit: எல்லா செலவுகளுக்கும் பிறகு மீதம்.
ஒரு காலாண்டு அல்ல, பல ஆண்டு போக்கைப் பாருங்கள்.

quiz.q: A company has revenue of ₹500 crore and net profit of ₹50 crore. What is its net margin?

lessons.title: P/E ratio and valuation
lessons.body:
The **P/E ratio** = share price ÷ earnings per share (EPS). It tells you how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of yearly profit.

**Example:** price ₹500, EPS ₹25 → P/E of **20**.

A high P/E can mean investors expect fast growth, or that the share is expensive. A low P/E can mean it's cheap, or that the business has problems. **Compare with the company's own history and with similar companies**, not across unrelated sectors.

**Key idea:** a great company bought at too high a price can still be a poor investment.
ta: P/E = பங்கு விலை ÷ ஒரு பங்கின் வருமானம் (EPS).
அதே துறையில் உள்ள நிறுவனங்களுடன் ஒப்பிட்டுப் பாருங்கள்.

quiz.q: A share costs ₹300 and its EPS is ₹15. What is its P/E?

lessons.title: Debt and the balance sheet
lessons.body:
The **balance sheet** shows what a company owns (assets) and owes (liabilities). The difference is **shareholders' equity**.

**Debt-to-equity** = total debt ÷ equity. Debt ₹400 crore and equity ₹1,000 crore → **0.4**.

Some debt is normal, especially for banks, power and infrastructure companies. But very high debt makes a company fragile when interest rates rise or business slows.

**Key idea:** companies that can fund growth from their own cash are usually safer than those that keep borrowing.
ta: Balance sheet: சொத்துகள் (assets) மற்றும் கடன்கள் (liabilities).
Debt-to-equity = கடன் ÷ பங்குதாரர் மூலதனம்.
அதிக கடன் உள்ள நிறுவனங்கள் கடினமான காலங்களில் பாதிக்கப்படலாம்.

quiz.q: Debt is ₹200 crore and equity is ₹800 crore. What is debt-to-equity?

lessons.title: Moats: what makes a business last
lessons.body:
Warren Buffett popularised the idea of an **economic moat**: a lasting advantage that protects a business from competitors, like a moat around a castle.

Common moats: **strong brands** (customers pay more for them), **low cost** (can sell cheaper and still profit), **network effects** (more users make it more valuable), **switching costs** (hard for customers to leave), and **licences or scale**.

**Key idea:** ask, "Why will this company still be earning well in 10 years?" If you can't answer, be careful.
ta: Moat: போட்டியாளர்களிடமிருந்து நிறுவனத்தைப் பாதுகாக்கும் நீடித்த நன்மை.
வலுவான பிராண்ட், குறைந்த செலவு, network effect, மாறுவதில் சிரமம் போன்றவை moat-கள்.
'10 ஆண்டுகளுக்குப் பிறகும் இந்த நிறுவனம் ஏன் நன்றாக இருக்கும்?' என்று கேளுங்கள்.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an economic moat?
options: A strong brand customers keep paying more for

lessons.title: Mr. Market: don't let moods move you
lessons.body:
In *The Intelligent Investor*, Benjamin Graham imagines a business partner called **Mr. Market** who every day offers to buy or sell shares at a price. Some days he is euphoric and asks too much; other days he is gloomy and sells too cheap.

You don't have to trade with him. His mood is an **opportunity, not an instruction**.

**Key idea:** when markets fall sharply, ask whether the businesses changed, or only the mood.
ta: Benjamin Graham-இன் 'Mr. Market' உவமை: சந்தையின் மனநிலை தினமும் மாறுகிறது.
அவர் சொல்லும் விலைக்கு நீங்கள் வாங்கவோ விற்கவோ கட்டாயமில்லை.
சந்தை வீழ்ச்சியில்: வணிகம் மாறியதா, அல்லது மனநிலை மட்டும் மாறியதா?

quiz.q: According to the Mr. Market idea, how should you treat a sudden market crash?
options: As information about mood, and check whether the businesses actually changed

lessons.title: Margin of safety
lessons.body:
Graham's central idea: buy only when the price is **well below** your honest estimate of what the business is worth. The gap is your **margin of safety**.

It protects you from your own mistakes, because your estimate will sometimes be wrong.

For everyday investors, margin of safety also means: an emergency fund, no borrowed money for investing, and diversification.

**Key idea:** the goal is first to avoid big losses; growth follows.
ta: Margin of safety: மதிப்பை விட நன்றாக குறைந்த விலையில் வாங்குவது.
இது நம் தவறுகளிலிருந்து பாதுகாக்கும்.
கடன் வாங்கி முதலீடு செய்யாமல் இருப்பதும் ஒரு பாதுகாப்பு.

quiz.q: Why does a margin of safety help?
options: It protects you when your estimate of value turns out wrong
It lets you trade more often

lessons.title: Behaviour beats brilliance
lessons.body:
Morgan Housel's *The Psychology of Money* argues that **how you behave** with money matters more than how smart you are.

- **Fear and greed** make people buy high and sell low.
- **"Enough"**: knowing when you have enough stops you taking risks you don't need.
- **Room for error**: plan so that bad luck does not wipe you out.
- **Reasonable beats rational**: a plan you can stick to beats a perfect plan you abandon.

**Key idea:** the hardest part of investing is staying calm when everyone else isn't.
ta: பணத்தில் அறிவை விட நடத்தையே முக்கியம்.
பயமும் பேராசையும் உயர்ந்த விலையில் வாங்கி, குறைந்த விலையில் விற்க வைக்கின்றன.
நீங்கள் தொடர்ந்து பின்பற்றக்கூடிய எளிய திட்டமே சிறந்தது.

quiz.q: Which habit most often hurts investors' returns?

lessons.title: Small habits, automatic wealth
lessons.body:
James Clear's *Atomic Habits* shows that small actions repeated consistently create big results, the same maths as compounding.

Apply it to money:
- **Make it automatic:** set your SIP for the day after salary arrives.
- **Make it easy:** start with an amount that doesn't hurt, even ₹500.
- **Make it visible:** track your net worth once a month, not your portfolio every hour.
- **Step up** your SIP by 10% every year.

**Key idea:** consistency for 20 years beats brilliance for 2.
ta: சிறிய பழக்கங்கள் தொடர்ந்தால் பெரிய முடிவுகள் வரும்.
சம்பளம் வந்த மறுநாள் SIP தானாக செல்லும்படி அமைக்கவும்.
ஒவ்வொரு ஆண்டும் SIP-ஐ 10% உயர்த்துங்கள்.

quiz.q: What's the best way to make investing a habit?
options: Wait for the perfect market moment
Automate a SIP right after payday

lessons.title: Assets vs liabilities
lessons.body:
Robert Kiyosaki's *Rich Dad Poor Dad* popularised a simple test: an **asset** puts money into your pocket; a **liability** takes money out.

Shares that pay dividends, a fund that grows, or skills that raise your income are assets. A car loan for a car you can't afford, or EMIs on gadgets, drain cash every month.

**Key idea:** before a big purchase, ask whether it builds your future or only your present. Use the EMI calculator to see what a loan really costs.
ta: Asset உங்களுக்கு பணம் தரும்; Liability உங்களிடமிருந்து பணம் எடுக்கும்.
வருமானம் தரும் பங்குகள், திறன்கள் assets; தேவையற்ற EMI-கள் liabilities.
பெரிய செலவுக்கு முன், இது எதிர்காலத்தை உருவாக்குகிறதா என்று யோசியுங்கள்.
